items.title: GitHub App improvements for least privilege and management
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: We’re releasing several GitHub Apps improvements today that help developers move off of classic PATs, improve GitHub App management, and request fewer sensitive permissions. We’ve also made it easier for repository administrators to use apps that their administrators have approved and updated the GitHub App credential management UI in advance of our planned workload federation features. New repository creation and installation management permissions Two new repository fine-grained permissions have been added, available to both fine-grained PATs and GitHub Apps. repository_creation:write: Allows the caller to create a repository in the account where it’s granted. installation_repositories: write: Allows the caller to add or remove that repository from an installation in the organization. Create a repository without repository_administration You can now use the repository_creation:write permission to create repositories without needing the broader repository_administration:write permission. Previously, an app or PAT needed repository_administration:write to create a repository. That permission also grants other repository administration features like deletion and transfer. This could lead to administrators rejecting apps, banning PATs with this permission, or having to accept the over-privilege risk. The new permission supports a least-privilege approach by granting only the ability to create repositories. When the repository is created, the app or user that created it will be given access to it. An app using this permission still requires an organization administrator to install the app. See the API docs for repository creation in organizations, from a template, for the current user, with a fork, and via GraphQL. Manage installation repositories with an app or fine-grained PAT The Add a repository to an installation organization-level API and its corresponding removal API now support GitHub Apps and fine-grained PATs. Previously, these APIs only supported the coarse-
items.why_it_matters: New least-privilege GitHub App permissions and help moving off classic PATs tighten CI and agent access to client repos, ahead of planned workload federation.

items.title: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles in public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Tags and branches can move after you review a workflow, so a later run might execute different code. Lockfiles let you keep those references in your workflow while running the exact commits you locked. Editor’s note (October 14th, 2026): Updated which plans have access to this public preview. If an action is compromised, a moved tag or branch can introduce malicious code into your workflow without a change to your repository. Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes by keeping workflow runs tied to the commits you locked. Locking does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe, so review dependencies before locking them. Install the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to create and maintain your workflow lockfile. With the extension, you can: Pin your dependencies: Generate .github/workflows/actions.lock with reviewable commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, as well as reusable workflow dependencies. Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. Once onboarded, a workflow must have lockfile entries for its dependencies, and GitHub Actions runs the recorded commits. Keep workflow runs consistent: GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and uses its recorded commit, even if a tag or branch moves. Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that the lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check. The Require lockfile policy is also available in public preview. Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can require workflows to use lockfiles across their enterprise, organization, or repository. Keep locked dependencies up to date with Dependabot Dependabot helps you keep your GitHub Actions dependencies up to date. When it opens a version update for an action in a work
items.why_it_matters: GitHub Actions lockfiles pin workflow dependencies to exact commits, so a moved or compromised action tag cannot change what runs. This is directly applicable supply-chain hardening for our CI and client repos.

items.title: HydraFusion updates and new Max option
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: HydraFusion has an updated model pool, improved orchestration workflows, and introduces HydraFusion Max. Both HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max are available across VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, and GitHub Copilot CLI and remain in research preview. HydraFusion orchestrates multiple models to produce a single response, bringing together their strengths so you don’t have to choose an individual model for each task. What’s new in HydraFusion Latest frontier models: HydraFusion and HydraFusion Max draw from a pool that now includes Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna. The models used for each task vary based on the orchestration workflow. Reasoning effort tailored to each step: Previously, HydraFusion only used each model’s default reasoning effort. With this update, it explicitly tailors effort to each stage, using medium effort for initial drafts and high effort for review. This keeps drafting efficient while dedicating deeper reasoning to checking and improving the work. Optimized Cascade and Critique workflows: Cascade: Previously used an initial model to solve the task, with escalation to a stronger model when needed. It can now include a judging step that inspects the initial work and requests a repair only when needed. Critique: Previously relied heavily on text summaries. It now relies more on tools to inspect the actual workspace directly. Critique now also uses parallel critic models to inspect work. Introducing HydraFusion Max HydraFusion Max is built on the same architecture and uses the same workflow techniques as HydraFusion, but is tuned for frontier capability on more demanding tasks. It applies higher reasoning efforts where depth and thoroughness matter most, while still using orchestration to consider token efficiency. Option Description Typical use case HydraFusion Balanced approach with moderate token savings. Agentic tasks that require a balance of speed, cost, and performance. items.excerpt: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist! Tags: google, ai, generative-ai, llms, llm, gemini, llm-pricing, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, llm-release

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.excerpt: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied: Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Cl
items.why_it_matters: Anthropic went from 2,500 to 30,000 merged changes a day and built its own Git alternative. It is a signal of where high-volume agentic delivery is heading and the source control strain it brings.

items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.excerpt: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history, game-design, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, ai-ethics, coding-agents
items.why_it_matters: AI-powered decompilation is getting easy, which weakens obscurity as protection for shipped client code and binaries. Worth knowing when advising clients on IP and security.

items.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.author: Brandon Anderson

Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding, or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is. Their substack — or at least Owl Posting’s1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI.So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules.2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing.It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint, blog, and open dataset. We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. items.title: Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna's million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason's journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna. We discuss: - Why Dyna-2 was trained on over one million hours of human video - World-action models: predicting future video to guide physical robot actions - Diffusion transformers, flow matching, and real-time robotic control - How robots learn new tasks with as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations - Why robotics has no equivalent of the internet and data remains its biggest scaling challenge - Human egocentric video, robot demonstrations, and cross-embodiment transfer - Synthetic environments, simulation, and models that generate their own train

items.title: From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: From a four-billion-measurement Kaggle competition to models that recognize a molecule’s chemist, Leash Bio is testing what AI actually learns about chemistry. Co-founder and CEO Ian Quigley joins Brandon Anderson and RJ Honicky to explain how Leash makes DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) produce clean, reproducible protein–small-molecule binding data—and why collecting the right experiments matters as much as choosing a model. We go deep on hidden shortcuts in public datasets, Hermes’ comparison with Boltz, and the protein mutations that expose memorization. Ian explains how Leash’s measured chemical landscapes can become a sandbox for reasoning agents, with rapid experimental feedback and thousands of medicinal chemistry campaigns. We also examine the limits of DELs, moving hits toward medicines, the economics of AI drug discovery, and the experimental bottlenecks that still need solving. We discuss: • How DNA-encoded libraries use barcodes and sequencing to screen millions of molecules • Catching DNA-binding artifacts with multiple barcodes per molecule • Why Leash prioritizes reproducible measurements across many protein targets • The BELKA Kaggle competition: four billion measurements, around 2,000 teams, and no better than chance on an unseen chemical library • Clever Hans in ChEMBL: learning who made a molecule instead of the chemistry • Hermes, simple baselines, careful data splits, and comparisons with Boltz • Activity cliffs, engineered protein mutations, and models that memorize protein “nicknames” • Agents reasoning about structure–activity relationships in plain English • More than 10,000 medicinal chemistry campaigns in a weekend • Going from DEL hits to mouse PK/PD, and the case for pills on difficult targets • The Kosuri paradox: if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? • Experimental know-how, detecting misfolded proteins, and scaling purification — Show Notes: https://www.latent.space/publish/post/220316507 Ian Quigley — Leash Bio • Linke
items.why_it_matters: Video version of the Leash Bio drug-discovery interview. Domain-specific ML research with no near-term engineering impact for us.

items.title: How to kill your SaaS: what we learned replacing a $43K/yr tool with AI agents
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: A SaaS vendor quoted us $43,000 a year to run speakers for my @AIdotEngineer conferences. That would be fine if it delivered the qualitySo we asked builders to clone it with coding agents, open source, eval by the people who'd actually use it: our human events team. 72 teams submitted. This is what we learned: how the best builders split work between Claude Code and Codex, why our own AI judge ranked the winner 19th, the three things almost every clone got wrong, and why owning software is a different job from building it. Winners 🥇 $10,000: Valentin De Matos, OpenRostrum: https://openrostrum.com · https://github.com/openrostrum/openrostrum 🥈 $5,000: Yazin, Conferencer: https://conferencer.cc · https://github.com/yazinsai/conferencer 🥉 $1,000: Marko Kraemer, Trackstage: https://trackstage.app · https://github.com/markokraemer/trackstage Valentin's agent guardrails template: https://github.com/Thytu/agent-rules Harness Engineering 101: https://thytu.com/posts/harness-engineering Full report: https://kms.latent.space Want to sponsor the next Kill My SaaS?
